lesson.lesson_summary: A word does not always belong to the same word class. Its job in a sentence helps us identify its class. Learn to use sentence meaning, position, and grammatical function to classify words correctly, even when the same word performs different jobs.

learning_objectives.description: Explain why a word must be understood in its sentence context before its word class can be identified.
success_criteria: Explain that a word can perform different grammatical jobs.
Recognise that the same spelling can belong to different word classes.

learning_objectives.description: Identify the word class of a word by examining its job in a sentence.
success_criteria: Identify the grammatical function of a target word.
Use surrounding words and sentence meaning to classify it.
Distinguish between a word's meaning and its grammatical job.

learning_objectives.description: Classify words that can belong to different word classes in different sentences.
success_criteria: Recognise nouns and verbs that share the same spelling.
Recognise adjectives and verbs that share the same spelling.
Recognise words that can function as more than two word classes.

learning_objectives.description: Distinguish between word classes that are easily confused in real sentences.
success_criteria: Distinguish prepositions from conjunctions and adverbs through their sentence functions.

learning_objectives.description: Apply contextual word classification when analysing complete sentences.
success_criteria: Classify highlighted words in unfamiliar sentences.
Explain why a word belongs to a particular class.
Correct incorrect word classifications using sentence evidence.

learning_dimensions.dimension: Identifying Word Classes Through Sentence Function
Recognising Words with Multiple Grammatical Jobs

pages.title: One Word, Different Jobs

content.text: Can one word do different jobs? Yes! A word can belong to different word classes in different sentences. Its job depends on how it is used.

examples.explanation: Drink names an action. It is a verb.
Drink names something you have. It is a noun.

pages.key_takeaway: A word's grammatical role can change from sentence to sentence.

pages.title: Context Gives the Clue

content.text: Context means the words and ideas around a word. They help us understand what the word is doing in a sentence.

examples.explanation: Fly tells us what the birds do. It is a verb.
Play names a performance. It is a noun.

pages.key_takeaway: Look at the whole sentence, not just one word.

pages.title: Same Word, Different Class

comparison_points: Help names something in the first sentence.
Help shows an action in the second sentence.
content.conclusion: The spelling stays the same, but the grammatical job changes.

pages.key_takeaway: Word class depends on grammatical function.

content.text: To identify a word class, ask what the word does in the sentence. Does it name something, show an action, describe something, or give more information?

items: Names a person, place, thing or idea: noun.
Shows an action or state: verb.
Adds information about an action or description: adverb.

examples.explanation: Small describes the noun puppy. It is an adjective.
Beautifully tells us how the bird sings. It is an adverb.

content.title: Look carefully
content.text: Do not classify a word only because of its spelling or ending. Check its actual job.
Read the sentence carefully. Find the highlighted word's job before choosing its word class.

pages.title: A Word Can Be a Noun or Verb

examples.explanation: Dance shows what the children do. It is a verb.
Dance names an event. It is a noun.

content.title: Remember
content.text: Many action words can also name activities or events.

pages.key_takeaway: A noun can name an action as an activity.

pages.title: Brush Has Two Jobs

examples.sentence: I brush my hair every morning.
examples.explanation: Brush tells us what action I perform. It is a verb.
Brush names an object. It is a noun.

pages.key_takeaway: Brush can name an object or show an action.

pages.title: Plant Has Different Jobs

examples.explanation: Plant names a living thing. It is a noun.
Plant tells us what action they perform. It is a verb.

content.title: Remember
content.text: The same spelling can name something in one sentence and express an action in another.

pages.key_takeaway: Plant can be a noun or a verb.

pages.title: Empty Can Change Its Job

examples.sentence: The empty box is on the floor.
examples.explanation: Empty describes the box. It is an adjective.
Empty tells us what action to perform. It is a verb.

content.title: Think about the job
content.text: Is empty describing something, or is it showing an action?

pages.key_takeaway: An adjective can also function as a verb.

pages.title: Straight Can Be Two Classes

examples.explanation: Straight describes the line. It is an adjective.
Straight tells us the direction in which to walk. It is an adverb.

content.title: Important
content.text: Some adverbs do not end in -ly. Straight can be an adverb when it gives information about direction.

pages.key_takeaway: A word's ending does not always reveal its class.

pages.title: Since Has Different Jobs

examples.explanation: Since connects the time period 2020 with the action of living here. It is a preposition.

examples.sentence: Since you arrived, everything has changed.
examples.explanation: Since introduces a clause containing a subject and a verb. It is a conjunction.

content.title: A useful clue
content.text: Look at what comes after since. A noun phrase or a full clause can help identify its job.

pages.key_takeaway: Since can be a preposition or a conjunction.

pages.title: Round Can Be Three Classes

examples.explanation: Around shows the relationship between the sitting and the table. It is a preposition.
Around gives more information about where the children stood. It is an adverb.

examples.sentence: We played a round of chess.
examples.explanation: Round names one stage of a game. It is a noun.

pages.key_takeaway: One spelling can perform several grammatical jobs.

pages.title: Noun or Verb?

items.label: Noun
items.description: Names a person, place, thing or idea.

comparison_points: Cook names a person in the first sentence.
Cook shows an action in the second sentence.
content.conclusion: Ask whether the word names something or shows what someone does.

pages.key_takeaway: Naming and doing are different grammatical jobs.

pages.title: Describing Words: Adjective or Adverb?

items.label: Adverb
items.description: Can describe a verb, adjective or another adverb.

comparison_points: Late describes the noun bus in the first sentence.
Late tells us when the bus arrived in the second sentence.
content.conclusion: Check what the describing word is connected to.

mistake.reason: Patiently describes how he explains. It is an adverb in this sentence.

pages.key_takeaway: Check whether a word describes a noun or modifies an action.

content.text: Never guess a word class from a word alone. Read the whole sentence. Notice the words around it and understand what job it performs.

items: Find the job of the highlighted word.
Choose the word class that matches its job.

content.text: The same word may appear in different sentences. Identify its word class separately each time.

pages.title: Avoid These Mistakes

mistake.incorrect: Words ending in -ly are always adverbs.
mistake.correct: Words ending in -ly are often adverbs, but some are adjectives.
mistake.reason: In a friendly person, friendly is an adjective. In she speaks kindly, kindly is an adverb.

mistake.incorrect: Dance is always a verb because it means an activity.
mistake.correct: Dance can be a noun or a verb.
mistake.reason: In They dance, it is a verb. In Their dance was beautiful, it is a noun.

pages.key_takeaway: Meaning and sentence function work together.

pages.title: The Context Rule

content.text: You have learned that the same word can perform different grammatical jobs in different sentences. Its word class depends on how it works in context.

items: A word can belong to more than one word class.
Its spelling does not always reveal its class.
Its meaning and grammatical function provide clues.

pages.key_takeaway: Context is the key to word classification.

question_bank.prompt: In which sentence is the word help a noun?
question_bank.explanation: In I need some help, help names something that is needed. It is a noun.

question_bank.prompt: Identify the word class of little in: The little puppy slept.
question_bank.explanation: Little describes the noun puppy. Therefore, it is an adjective.

question_bank.prompt: What is the word class of soundly in: The baby slept soundly?
question_bank.explanation: Soundly tells us how the baby slept. It modifies the verb slept, so it is an adverb.

question_bank.prompt: What is the word class of brush in: This brush has soft bristles?
question_bank.explanation: Brush names an object. Therefore, it is a noun.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is the word cook in: My uncle is a cook?
question_bank.explanation: Cook names a person whose job is preparing food. It is a noun.

question_bank.prompt: In the sentence I have lived here since 2020, what is since?
question_bank.explanation: Since connects the time expression 2020 with the clause I have lived here. It is a preposition.

question_bank.prompt: What is the word class of straight in: Draw a straight line?
question_bank.explanation: Straight describes the line. It is an adjective.

question_bank.prompt: What is the word class of round in: We played a round of cards?
question_bank.explanation: Round names one part or stage of the game. It is a noun.

question_bank.prompt: Read both sentences: (1) They dance every evening. (2) Their dance was enjoyable. What is the word class of dance in sentence 1 and sentence 2?

options.text: Verb in sentence 1 and noun in sentence 2
Noun in sentence 1 and verb in sentence 2

question_bank.explanation: In sentence 1, dance shows an action, so it is a verb. In sentence 2, dance names an activity, so it is a noun.

question_bank.prompt: A word always belongs to the same word class in every sentence.
question_bank.explanation: A word can perform different grammatical jobs in different sentences. Its word class depends on its use.

question_bank.prompt: What part of speech is the word straight in: Walk straight ahead?
question_bank.explanation: Straight tells us the direction in which to walk. It modifies the verb walk, so it is an adverb.

question_bank.prompt: In which sentence is empty a verb?

options.text: The empty box is on the floor.

question_bank.explanation: In sentence B, empty tells someone what action to perform. It is a verb.

question_bank.prompt: In the sentence I waited until the bell rang, what is until?
question_bank.explanation: Until joins the main clause with the clause the bell rang. It is a subordinating conjunction.

question_bank.prompt: Match each highlighted word with its word class in the given sentence.
question_bank.explanation: Brush names an object or shows an action. Straight describes a line or tells us the direction of movement.

question_bank.prompt: Correct the sentence to mean that the bus did not arrive on time: The bus arrived lately.
question_bank.explanation: Late tells us when the bus arrived and functions as an adverb. Lately means recently and does not express the meaning of arriving after the expected time.

question_bank.prompt: In the sentence The children stood around, what is around?
question_bank.explanation: Around gives information about where the children stood. There is no object after it, so it functions as an adverb here.

question_bank.prompt: In which sentence is plant a verb?

options.text: A small plant grew near the wall.

question_bank.explanation: In sentence B, plant tells us what action they perform. It is a verb.
Many adverbs end in -ly, but some do not. Fast, hard, and well can also function as adverbs.

question_bank.prompt: What is the word class of sweet in: The flowers smell sweet?
question_bank.explanation: Sweet describes the flowers, not the action of smelling. It is an adjective.

cross_references.reason: This lesson uses previously introduced word classes to show how their grammatical jobs change with context. A complete introduction to all eight classes belongs to the preceding lessons.
Understanding sentence structure can help learners identify grammatical functions. A detailed study of these sentence elements requires a separate lesson.
Some verb forms can function as nouns or perform other grammatical roles. Their detailed classification requires a separate lesson.
Some words change grammatical class without changing their spelling. The broader process of conversion and word formation requires a separate lesson.
